Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense, used of an alert condition and, by ordinary grammatical extension, of an alert person. The still-and-alert pairing is attributed to Yongjia Xuanjue's Verse on Stopping, while the Chan record also preserves criticism of Ruiyan Shiyan's command and names the pair itself as a fetter. The target remains the attested “alert” or “awake.” Compare “still” (寂寂), “master-in-charge” (主人公), and “playing with spirit-ghosts” (弄精魂).

Senses.Explanation: Alert or wide-awake. The headword occurs 1,323 times in 275 allowlisted texts. One major deployment is the command “stay awake” or “stay alert” (惺惺著, 169 occurrences). Ruiyan Shiyan's case has him call “Master!” to himself, answer “Yes!”, then say, “Stay awake; after this do not be fooled by anyone” (主人公……諾……惺惺著，以後莫被人瞞). The same word describes an alert person: Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts an alert person, for whom moving, not moving, or both are acceptable, with a person who is not alert, for whom none is acceptable (惺惺底人……未惺惺底人). A second major deployment is the fixed pair “still and alert” or “alert and still” (寂寂惺惺 / 惺惺寂寂, 47 / 36 occurrences). Yongjia Xuanjue's Verse on Stopping defines alert as not producing the signs of dull abiding or blank indeterminacy (惺惺謂不生昏住無記等相), then ranks alert-and-still as right, blank-and-still as wrong, still-and-alert as right, and scattered-and-alert as wrong (惺惺寂寂是，無記寂寂非，寂寂惺惺是，亂想惺惺非). Later records also criticize these deployments. Zhanran Yuancheng reports that all quarters called Ruiyan's self-address “playing with spirit-ghosts” (諸方謂其弄精魂). Fangrong Tongxi reverses the case by saying Ruiyan's house-master called Ruiyan rather than the reverse. Haiyin Zhaoru names still-and-alert among fetters, paired with torpor and scattering (被寂寂惺惺、昏沉散亂縛). The entry therefore keeps the attested gloss “alert” while preserving both the formulas and the named criticisms.
